---
title: Use Marfa with AI agents
description: Connect Claude Code, Codex or an agent that runs unattended to your instance, so it can find, read and save your items with only the access you give it.
---

An agent on your computer connects to your instance's [MCP server](/marfa-mcp-server) and gets tools to find, read, save and change your items. **Every tool call is made with the agent's own credential**, so it reaches only what you approved, and you can cut it off at any time. If you installed the Marfa plugin from [Connect your agent](/connect-your-agent), its `connect` skill does the first steps below for you. [Agents, the CLI and MCP](/agents-cli-and-mcp) explains the choices.

## Connect the agent

Without the plugin, add the server with your instance's address followed by `/mcp`, then sign in. `/mcp` finds, reads, saves and changes items; **connect `/mcp/schema` or `/mcp/admin` only when the agent shapes types or runs the instance**, as [Endpoints](/marfa-mcp-server#endpoints) describes.

<Tabs items={["Claude Code", "Codex"]}>
<Tab value="Claude Code">

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user marfa https://marfa.example.com/mcp
```

Then run `/mcp` in a session and choose **marfa** to sign in. `--scope user` adds the server for every project of yours; leave it out to add it for this project only.

</Tab>
<Tab value="Codex">

```bash
codex mcp add marfa --url https://marfa.example.com/mcp
codex mcp login marfa
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

Your browser opens your instance's approval page. Sign in as the owner if you aren't already. **Full access** gives the agent what it asked for, and **Choose access** lets you give less, such as read and edit on notes and nothing else. [Approve an app](/run/manage-apps#approve-an-app) describes the page.

The agent then calls `marfa_overview`, which answers with the types, tags and views it can reach. If it later needs access you didn't approve, the instance tells its client which scope to ask for, and a client that supports this asks you to approve it.

The computer that runs the agent must reach the instance at its address: over `https`, such as an address on your tailnet, or at `http://localhost` on the same machine. [Install the server](/run/install#choose-how-its-reached) covers the choices.

## Connect an agent that runs unattended

An agent that runs on a schedule, with nobody to approve it in a browser, uses a key instead. **Give each agent a key of its own**, holding only what it needs. This key reads and writes notes, reads tasks, and stops working after 30 days:

```bash
marfa keys create --label nightly-digest --source nightly-digest \
  --type-permission core.note=write \
  --type-permission core.task=read \
  --expires-in 30d
```

Run it with a credential that holds `keys.mint`, or as the owner on the instance's machine with `--socket`. The CLI prints the key, which begins `marfa_k1_`, once. **The source, `nightly-digest`, is stamped on every item the agent creates**, so you can tell its work from yours. [Manage keys](/run/manage-keys) covers what else a key can hold.

Put the key in `MARFA_API_KEY` in the agent's environment, from your secrets manager, and have the client send it as a Bearer header:

<Tabs items={["Claude Code", "Codex"]}>
<Tab value="Claude Code">

```json title=".mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "marfa": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://marfa.example.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${MARFA_API_KEY}" }
    }
  }
}
```

Claude Code reads `${MARFA_API_KEY}` from the environment, so the key stays out of the file.

</Tab>
<Tab value="Codex">

```bash
codex mcp add marfa --url https://marfa.example.com/mcp --bearer-token-env-var MARFA_API_KEY
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Use the CLI instead

A coding agent that runs shell commands can also use the [CLI](/cli), which reaches every operation, with a key of its own. Write a [profile](/cli#name-a-server-with-a-profile) whose `key_command` reads the key from your secrets manager, so the key is never in a file:

```toml title="profiles.toml"
[example]
url = "https://marfa.example.com"
key_command = ["op", "read", "op://Private/Marfa/agent-key"]
```

Then set `MARFA_PROFILE=example` and `MARFA_NO_KEYCHAIN=1` in the environment the agent runs its commands in. **With the keychain off, a command that names no profile or server is refused**, so the agent can't reach whichever instance the keychain made current. Each write also prints which instance it changed on standard error.

Tell the agent how to use it in its instructions file:

```markdown title="AGENTS.md"
## Marfa

My notes are in Marfa. Use the `marfa` CLI, with `--json` on every command.

- Learn what the key reaches: `marfa overview --json`
- Find notes: `marfa search "<words>" --type core.note --json`
- Read one: `marfa items get <id> --json`
- To change one, read it first, then pass its `version` to `marfa items update`.
```

With `--json`, a refusal is one JSON object on the last line of standard error, and the exit code says whether to try again. [Exit codes](/cli#exit-codes) lists them.

## See what it did, and stop it

**Every write is in the [audit log](/run/audit-log)** with the credential that made it, and a write through a tool also carries `"via": "mcp"`. `marfa items list --source nightly-digest` lists what a keyed agent created.

You can **stop an agent at once**. Revoke its key with `marfa keys revoke <key id>`, or disconnect a signed-in agent on the **Connected apps** page, as [Authenticate](/build/authenticate#revoke-access) describes. Its next request is refused.

## Let the agent read these docs

An agent that builds on Marfa does better with the current docs than from memory. Connect the docs MCP server, or point the agent at [`/llms.txt`](/llms.txt), as [Docs for agents](/docs-for-agents) shows.
